1. Core Clinical Tension: A 44-year-old immunocompetent woman presenting with chronic, 1-year progressive monoarthritis of the right elbow with purulent sinus tract discharge, constitutional symptoms, and joint subluxation with osteolysis. The clinical tension centers on distinguishing atypical monoarticular mycobacterial osteoarthritis from common pyogenic bacterial septic arthritis, synovial sarcoma, or rheumatoid monoarthritis, particularly in the absence of pulmonary involvement.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The presentation ends after initial triage history, local physical examination, plain radiographs of the elbow and chest, and baseline inflammatory markers/CBC, immediately prior to microbiological culture for acid-fast bacilli and open surgical arthrotomy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Differentiating tuberculous osteoarthritis from pyogenic septic arthritis (ruled out by indolent 1-year course, minimal systemic leukocytosis, and sterile pyogenic cultures), synovial neoplastic pseudotumor / sarcoma (ruled out by histopathologic identification of caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells), and inflammatory monoarthritis.
case_prompt: A 44-year-old woman from a rural area in Tunisia with unfavorable socioeconomic conditions and no prior medical history presented to the emergency service with a 1-year history of progressive pain, swelling, and functional limitation of the right elbow. Over the preceding year, she had also noted fatigue, night sweats, low-grade fever, and general physical deterioration. Six months prior to presentation, a spontaneous sinus tract developed over the elbow with persistent purulent drainage. She reported no prior history of trauma or septic inoculation. On physical examination, the right elbow was markedly swollen (circumference 10 cm), erythematous, warm, and exquisitely tender, with range of motion severely limited to 30° to 80°. No other joints were affected. Plain radiographs of the right elbow showed marginal periarticular osteolysis and elbow subluxation. A plain chest radiograph was normal. Laboratory investigations revealed a white blood cell count of 11 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein of 40 mg/L (reference: 0–5 mg/L), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 37 mm/h (reference: 0–20 mm/h).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to local erythema, heat, and purulent fistulization, but ruled out by the chronic 1-year progression, normal white blood cell count, and characteristic marginal periarticular osteolysis on plain films.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Standard radiological assessment, including anteroposterior and lateral plain radiographs of the right elbow, showed marginal periarticular osteolysis and elbow subluxation

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered intraoperatively when hypertrophic synovial tissue mimicked a neoplastic lesion, but histopathology demonstrated granulomatous caseation rather than malignant mesenchymal neoplasia.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Hypertrophic synovium resembling a pseudotumor, bone erosion, and minimal purulent drainage were also observed

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Microbiological isolation of acid-fast bacilli from draining sinus pus and histopathological confirmation of necrotizing granulomas with Langhans giant cells established the diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The pus sample was cultured for bacteria, including acid-fast bacilli (AFB), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis was identified, confirming the diagnosis of tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Distilled admission teaching case for tuberculous osteoarthritis of the elbow. Breakpoint enforced prior to AFB culture and arthrotomy. Zero pathogen spoilers. Verbatim quotes validated.
